title: The shuffle, partitioning and joins
goal: By the end, you can explain what a shuffle writes to disk and reads back, choose how Spark splits rows into partitions and how many partitions to ask for, and read a join's plan to see whether it moves the big table or copies the small one.
opening:
Picture the company that runs the café's card payments. Every hour, a report adds up what each shop took, and it takes about 6 minutes. Then the owners want totals per kind of shop: cafés, bookshops, grocers. Only the shops table knows each shop's kind, so a teammate adds one line, a join that matches each payment with its shop. The report now takes 25 minutes.

The shops table is tiny, so this makes no sense at first. It's easy to blame the matching, because that's the work the new line shows. The cost hides in a step the code never mentions. Spark, the program that runs the report across many computers, can only match two rows that sit on the same computer, so first it moves rows.

In The Spark execution model, we met that moving step, the shuffle, where Spark cuts a job into stages. In this lesson, we'll open it up. We'll find its files, count its cost, choose how rows get split, and pick a join that leaves the payments in place. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The report joins a million payments with a table of 500 shops. Spark's plan for this join moves the rows of both tables, so that each shop's payments and the shop's own row end up on the same computer. How many of the million payments does it move?
options: None: the shops table is small, so Spark moves only the shops
Only the payments whose shop is in the shops table
warmup.why: When both tables are moved by shop number, every payment is written out and sent to the computer that handles its shop, whatever the size of the other table. The demo in the last section counted 1,000,500 rows moved for the join: every payment plus every shop. The tempting first option describes a different plan, which copies the small table to every computer and moves no payment at all. A small table only helps if Spark picks that plan, and the last section shows when it does.

sections.h: Moving each row to its key: what a shuffle writes and reads
sections.body:
Spark works on a DataFrame, a table with named columns whose rows are cut into partitions: slices that can be worked on at the same time. Ours holds a million made-up payments in 4 partitions. Each row has a payment number, a shop number and an amount in cents. (The code calls a shop a merchant, so the shop number is `merchant_id`.) We ask Spark to cut the table again, so that each shop's payments sit together:

```kotlin
payments.repartition(4, col("merchant_id"))
```

Almost every row must move, because every partition holds payments for almost every shop. A piece of work that handles one partition is a task. Map tasks read the old partitions, and reduce tasks build the new ones, names from lesson 3, HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived. Each row must reach the one reduce task that owns its shop, and that task runs later, maybe on another computer.

Picture a post office at the end of the day. Four clerks each hold a sack of letters from all over town, and four vans wait outside, one per district. Version 1: each clerk carries every letter straight to its van. That breaks twice. A van may not be there yet: reduce tasks start only when the map tasks' stage is over. (A stage, from The Spark execution model, is a stretch of work between two shuffles.) And if a van breaks down, the letters inside are lost, and every clerk must send them again.

Version 2: write first, fetch later. Each clerk sorts the letters into four pigeonholes on a shelf, one per van, with a note saying where each one starts. When every clerk is done, each driver collects one pigeonhole from every shelf.

Spark does the same. Each map task works out each row's reduce task with `hash(merchant_id) mod 4`. A hash is a function that turns a key into a number, the same number every time. `mod 4` keeps the remainder after dividing by 4: 0, 1, 2 or 3. The map task sorts its rows by that number and writes them to its own computer's disk, in the folder named by `spark.local.dir`. It writes one data file with four blocks back to back, and a small index file that says where each block starts and ends. Then each reduce task fetches its block from every map task's file, from the same computer or over the network. This is Spark's sort-based shuffle.

The Try it shows the files: four `.data` files of about 3.4 MB, and four `.index` files of 40 bytes each. 40 bytes is five numbers of 8 bytes, `[0, 856322, 1767340, 2547897, 3421874]`. So reduce task 1 reads bytes 856,322 to 1,767,340 of each data file.

Now count the cost for M map tasks and R reduce tasks. The map side writes M data files, and the reduce side fetches M x R blocks. Each row is serialized (turned into bytes), compressed (`spark.shuffle.compress` is on by default), written to disk, read back, sent over the network and turned back into a row. In the demo, a million rows became 13.7 MB of shuffle write, and the reduce side read the same 13.7 MB. With 1,000 map tasks and 1,000 reduce tasks, that's a million blocks to fetch, most of them small.

Here the post office picture breaks. A clerk clears the shelf at night, but Spark keeps shuffle files until it cleans up the DataFrame that made them. So a failed reduce task only fetches again, and running the same DataFrame twice can skip its first stage.

**Every shuffle writes the whole table to disk and reads it back. Run as few as you can.** Most of this lesson is about choosing well. First, let's see what all those small blocks cost.

aside.title: Isn't Spark supposed to work in memory?
aside.body: Inside a stage, it does: a task reads a batch of rows, works on it in memory and moves on, and that's where much of Spark's speed comes from. Between stages, it writes to disk on purpose. The reduce tasks start later and may run on other computers, and a file on disk survives a task that fails. The operating system, the program that runs all the others, also keeps recently written files in memory for a while, so a small shuffle often never waits for the disk itself. So "in memory" describes the work inside a stage, not the handover between stages.

sections.h: Why small blocks make a shuffle slow, and two ways around it
sections.body:
Look again at the M x R blocks. Each map task splits its output into R blocks, so a block's size is a map task's output divided by R. The more reduce tasks, the smaller every block.

LinkedIn, the social network for jobs, measured what that does on its clusters (groups of computers that run jobs together) and published it in 2020 as the Magnet paper. Take 150 GB of map output from 1,000 map tasks. With R = 150, each block is about 1,000 KB; with R = 1,500, 100 KB; with R = 15,000, 10 KB. On LinkedIn's clusters the average block was only tens of KB, and billions of them were fetched every day from hard disks.

That matters because of how a hard disk reads. An arm moves over a spinning platter to the right spot, and each move takes several milliseconds. A big file read from start to end pays for one move; a million small blocks spread over the disk pay a million times. LinkedIn found that about 15% of its cluster's compute time went to tasks waiting for shuffle blocks. Moving 150 GB as 10 KB blocks through one shuffle service took about 4 hours. (A shuffle service is a program on each computer that hands out the shuffle blocks stored there to the reduce tasks that ask.)

Magnet merges the blocks before anyone fetches them. Each map task still writes its blocks locally, then pushes them to shuffle services on other computers. Each service appends every block for one reduce task into one file, like a depot that packs one big sack per van. A reduce task then reads a few large files from start to end, and the scheduler (the part of Spark that decides where each task runs) starts it near them. The same 150 GB moved in just over 5 minutes, and LinkedIn's real jobs ran almost 30% faster. Spark 3.2 shipped this as **push-based shuffle**. It's off by default (`spark.shuffle.push.enabled`), and it works only on one kind of cluster setup (Go deeper has the details).

The shuffle service matters for a second reason. Shuffle files live on the disk of the computer that ran the map task, inside an executor, the program on each worker computer that runs tasks. When an executor dies, or is removed because the cluster shrinks at a quiet hour, its shuffle files go with it, and its map tasks must run again. Spark's external shuffle service runs outside the executors, so it keeps serving those files after an executor is gone. It's the caretaker who keeps the shelves open when the clerk goes home.

Spark on Kubernetes, a popular system for running programs across many computers, has no such service yet; its docs list it as future work. **Remote shuffle services** fill the gap. Apache Celeborn and Apache Uniffle are free programs that keep shuffle data on servers of their own, so it outlives every executor. Then it's safe to add and remove executors during a job. It's also safe to use spot machines, cheap cloud computers that the provider can take back at short notice.

None of this changes how Spark picks a row's block. Next, we'll look at that rule, and at two others Spark can use instead.

sections.h: Hash, range or round robin: three ways to pick a row's partition
sections.body:
Every shuffle needs a rule that turns a row into a partition number, called the partitioner. `explain()` prints the plan, the list of steps Spark will run, and there a shuffle is a line that starts with `Exchange` and names its partitioner. Spark has three, and the post office has a picture for each.

Hash partitioning, `hashpartitioning(merchant_id, 4)`, is the one we've used: the partition is the key's hash mod 4. It's like sorting letters by a code worked out from the postcode. Equal keys always meet, which is what `groupBy` (gathering each key's rows, say to add them up), joins and `repartition(4, col("merchant_id"))` need. The sizes follow the keys: the demo's four partitions got 250,101, 265,871, 228,299 and 255,729 rows. A shop with a third of all payments would make one partition huge. One key with far more rows than the others is called skew, and the next lesson, The optimizer, AQE, skew and caching, deals with it.

Range partitioning, `rangepartitioning(amount_cents ASC, 4)`, is what `orderBy`, sorting the whole table, uses. Each partition holds one stretch of keys, like letters for streets A to F, then G to M. Here, partition 0 holds amounts 100 to 67,180, partition 1 holds 67,181 to 123,255, and so on. Sort each partition, read them in order, and the whole table is sorted, with no single task sorting everything. But where should the cuts go? Spark doesn't know how the amounts are spread, so it first runs a separate job that samples the data (reads a small part of it) to choose the cut points. That's why the demo's `orderBy` ran 2 jobs.

Round robin, `RoundRobinPartitioning(4)`, is what `repartition(4)` uses when you name no column. Rows are dealt out like cards, one to each partition in turn: exactly 250,000 each. Use it to even out lopsided partitions. It puts each key wherever the deal happens to send it, so it can't help a `groupBy`.

`coalesce(n)` is not a shuffle at all. It merges neighbouring partitions where they are: 0 and 1 become one, 2 and 3 another. No row goes to a shuffle file, so it's cheap. It can only lower the number of partitions, and the result can be uneven.

It also has a trap. `coalesce` is narrow, meaning each new partition needs only old partitions next to it, so it runs inside the stage before it (The Spark execution model). So `heavy.coalesce(1).write()` doesn't run the heavy work in many tasks and then merge. It runs that whole stage as one task. The demo's `coalesce(2)` ran its stage with 2 tasks instead of 4. When the work before it is heavy, `repartition(1)` is faster, because the heavy stage keeps all its tasks and only the last step runs alone.

| You want | Use | Shuffle |
|---|---|---|
| fewer output files after cheap work | `coalesce(n)` | none |
| equal partitions | `repartition(n)` | round robin |
| every row of a key in one partition | `repartition(n, col(k))` | hash |
| sorted output | `orderBy(k)` | range, plus a sampling job |

Next, we'll decide how many partitions to make.

code.title: PartitioningDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l07.demo

import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset
import org.apache.spark.sql.Row
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.max
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.min
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.spark_partition_id

/**
 * Five ways to change the partitions of 1,000,000 payments (4 input partitions). For each one it
 * prints the plan node that does it, how many jobs ran, and what ended up in each partition.
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val log = StageLog(spark)
    val p = payments(spark)
    val cases = listOf<Pair<String, Dataset<Row>>>(
        "groupBy(merchant_id).count()" to p.groupBy("merchant_id").count(),
        "orderBy(amount_cents)" to p.orderBy("amount_cents"),
        "repartition(4)" to p.repartition(4),
        "repartition(4, merchant_id)" to p.repartition(4, col("merchant_id")),
        "coalesce(2)" to p.coalesce(2),
    )
    for ((label, df) in cases) {
        val node = planLines(df, "Exchange", "Coalesce").firstOrNull() ?: "no Exchange"
        val (jobs, stages) = log.run { df.foreachPartition { rows: Iterator<Row> -> rows.forEach { _ -> } } }
        val perPartition = df.withColumn("p", spark_partition_id()).groupBy("p").count().orderBy("p").collectAsList()
        println(label)
        println("  plan:  $node")
        println("  ran:   ${jobs.size} job(s), tasks per stage ${stages.map { it.tasks }}")
        println("  rows per partition: ${perPartition.map { "%,d".format(it.getLong(1)) }}")
        if (label.startsWith("orderBy")) {
            val ranges = df.withColumn("p", spark_partition_id()).groupBy("p")
                .agg(min("amount_cents"), max("amount_cents")).orderBy("p").collectAsList()
            println("  amounts per partition: ${ranges.map { "${it.getLong(1)}..${it.getLong(2)}" }}")
        }
    }
    spark.stop()
}

Its ranges came out balanced by row count, give or take a few thousand rows, because a sample only estimates where the cuts should go. Round robin gave exactly 250,000 rows each. `coalesce(2)` has no `Exchange` and a single stage, and that stage ran 2 tasks, so the work before it, making up the payments, also ran in 2 tasks instead of 4.

sections.h: Choosing how many partitions a shuffle makes
sections.body:
Every shuffle needs a number of output partitions, and that number is also the number of reduce tasks. For joins and `groupBy`, Spark takes it from the setting `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`. The default is 200, whatever the size of the data.

Too many costs time on small data. The demo adds up a million payments per shop with three values of the setting. Each map task first adds up its own rows per shop: the partial sums of lesson 3's combiner. So every run moves the same 2,000 rows, 500 shops from each of 4 map tasks. With 4 shuffle partitions it took 53 ms. With 200, it took 221 ms. With 2,000, it took 854 ms.

Why would more tasks be slower for the same rows? Each reduce task has a fixed cost. The scheduler has to start it, and it has to fetch one block from every map task, even when the block holds a single row. 2,000 reduce tasks times 4 map tasks is 8,000 block fetches for 2,000 rows. Even the bytes grow, because each block is compressed on its own, with its own small header: the same rows took 20,633 bytes in 4 partitions and 116,064 in 2,000. (Spark isn't the first system to spend more on envelopes than on letters.)

Too few costs memory on big data. A 500 GB shuffle into 200 partitions gives each reduce task 2.5 GB to sort or add up. That doesn't fit in the memory one task gets, so the task spills: it writes sorted pieces to disk and merges them later, which is slow. Or it fails with an out-of-memory error. The same 500 GB in partitions of 64 MB would need about 7,800 of them.

So the right number depends on the data, and the data changes every night. Adaptive query execution (AQE), a part of Spark that's on by default and that the next lesson opens up, solves most of this while the job runs. When the map tasks finish, AQE knows the real size of every shuffle partition, and it merges small neighbours up to a target of 64 MB (`spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`). The demo's first three runs had AQE turned off. With it on, 2,000 partitions became one reduce task, in 65 ms.

Spark's tuning guide says to set a large starting number and let AQE pick the final one, because apart from skewed joins (next lesson), AQE only merges. **AQE can merge partitions but not split them. Start high.**

One more effect: when the reduce stage writes files, each task writes its own. A table written straight after a 200-partition shuffle gets up to 200 files per folder. That's the small-files problem from lesson 4, Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore.

So far we've moved one table. A join needs two tables to meet, and that's where choosing well pays the most.

Only the reduce side changes, and the time with it: 2,000 nearly empty tasks cost most of a second. AQE didn't change what the map side wrote; it changed how many tasks read it. Times depend on your computer and on what else it's doing, so compare the lines with each other. It also builds a new DataFrame for each run, because running the same one again would reuse its shuffle files.

sections.h: Joining two tables: move both, or copy the small one everywhere
sections.body:
A join matches the rows of two tables that share a key. `payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id")` gives each payment the row of its shop, which is how the opening's report learns each shop's kind. It has the `groupBy` problem twice over. Shop 42's payments sit in every payments partition, and shop 42's own row sits in one partition of the shops table. Some task has to hold both.

Version 1: shuffle both sides. Hash-partition the payments by `merchant_id` into N partitions, and the shops the same way into the same N. Shop 42 lands in the same partition number on both sides, so reduce task k gets every payment and every shop row for its keys. It sorts both sides by key and walks through them together, like merging two sorted piles of letters. That's the **sort-merge join**, Spark's default when both sides are big. It works at any size, because sorting can spill to disk. Its cost is a shuffle of both sides: in the demo, all 1,000,500 rows of the two tables (about 9.4 MB) and 4 stages.

A close cousin, the shuffled hash join, shuffles the same way but skips the sort. It builds a hash table from the smaller side of each partition: a lookup structure, like Kotlin's `HashMap`, that finds a key's row in one step. It's faster when that side fits in memory, and the hint `SHUFFLE_HASH` asks for it.

Version 2: leave the big side where it is. The driver (the program that plans the job and hands out tasks) collects the 500 shops and sends a copy to every executor. Each task builds a hash table from `merchant_id` to shop, streams its own payments through it and joins them in place. In the post office, that's photocopying the short list of districts for every clerk, so that no letter moves. This is the **broadcast hash join**: no payment is shuffled, nothing is sorted, and the join runs inside the first stage. The plan shows a `BroadcastExchange` under a `BroadcastHashJoin`. In the demo it took about half the time of the sort-merge join, and its only shuffle was the small one for the `groupBy` after the join. The stepper below shows both joins.

Spark broadcasts on its own when its size estimate for one side is below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, 10 MB by default. The estimate is the weak spot. After a filter, a join or a `groupBy`, Spark often can't tell how small a table has become. So it plans a sort-merge join for a table that would fit easily. That's what happened to the opening's report. Its shops were filtered to those still in business, Spark kept its estimate for the whole table (over 10 MB), and every payment went through a shuffle.

When you know a side is small, say so: `payments.join(broadcast(merchants), "merchant_id")`, or `/*+ BROADCAST(m) */` in a SQL query (SQL is the language most databases use for questions about tables). A hint is a request, and Spark can refuse it. A left outer join, for example, must keep every left row, even one with no match. So only its right side can be broadcast, whatever you ask for.

The photocopies are where the post office picture breaks. Copying a short list costs almost nothing, but a broadcast table passes through the driver, and a full copy lands in every executor's memory. Broadcast a 2 GB table to 100 executors and you've moved 200 GB, if the driver survives collecting it. Keep broadcasts to tables of tens of megabytes. AQE can also switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast join while the job runs, once the shuffle shows that one side is small. Spark's docs note that this is still slower than planning the broadcast from the start, and the next lesson shows why.

lab.title: Measure the shuffle, then fix a slow join
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The test session turns AQE off and sets `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` to -1, so Spark never broadcasts on its own. That's like a cluster whose size estimates are always too high.

Write `ShuffleMeter.onTaskEnd`. Spark calls it after every task with that task's numbers, its metrics: read the shuffle write and shuffle read numbers and add them to the four counters. The first three tests use the meter. A query with no shuffle must show zero, a `repartition` must count every row, and a `groupBy` must count one partial sum per shop per map task.

Look at `Joins.enrich`. It's the slow version, and the test shows that its plan is a `SortMergeJoin`. Fix it so that the plan is a `BroadcastHashJoin` with no `Exchange` at all. Your meter then proves that no payment moved.
Write `Layout.fewer`, `even` and `byKey`. One of them must not shuffle, one must give equal partitions, and one must let a later `groupBy(key)` run with no extra `Exchange`.
Run all eight tests until they pass.
hints: `taskEnd.taskMetrics()` can be null (for a task that failed); return early then. The numbers you need are `shuffleWriteMetrics().bytesWritten()` and `recordsWritten()`, and `shuffleReadMetrics().totalBytesRead()` and `recordsRead()`.
`org.apache.spark.sql.functions.broadcast(merchants)` marks a DataFrame to be copied to every task, whatever the threshold says.

`coalesce(n)` merges partitions without an `Exchange`. `repartition(n)` deals rows out round robin. `repartition(n, col(key))` hashes by the key, and a `groupBy(key)` after it finds its rows already where it needs them.

drill.title: Pick the join and the partitioning
drill.prompt: From memory, write the Kotlin for three jobs: (1) join 2 billion payments with a 3,000-row table of currencies so that no payment is shuffled; (2) write one day's filtered payments as about 10 files, without a shuffle; (3) cut a lopsided DataFrame into 64 equal partitions. Then say what `explain()` shows for each.

recap: A shuffle writes, then fetches: each map task writes one data file of R blocks plus an index to its own disk, and each reduce task fetches its block from every map task. That's M x R blocks in all, and small blocks are slow to fetch.

Hash partitioning puts equal keys together (`groupBy`, joins). Range partitioning gives sorted stretches and costs a sampling job (`orderBy`). Round robin gives equal sizes (`repartition(n)`). `coalesce(n)` merges partitions without a shuffle, but runs the stage before it in n tasks.
`spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (200 by default) sets the number of reduce tasks: too many wastes time on small data, and too few spills to disk on big data. With AQE on, start high and let AQE merge.

A sort-merge join shuffles both tables by key. A broadcast hash join copies the small table to every executor and moves none of the big one. Spark broadcasts below 10 MB by its own estimate, and `broadcast()` asks for it when the estimate is wrong.

The limit: every choice here rests on knowing sizes, and Spark's estimates after a filter are often wrong. A broadcast that's safe at 5 MB fills memory at 3 GB. The next lesson is about how Spark guesses sizes, and how it corrects itself.
closing:
We started with an hourly report that went from 6 minutes to 25 after one join. The shops table was small, but after its filter Spark couldn't tell, so it planned a sort-merge join and sent every payment through a shuffle. A `broadcast()` hint copies the shops to every task instead, and the payments stay where they are.

Run `JoinDemo` once more and read only the plans. Under each join, find what sits beneath the big table: an `Exchange` there means every one of its rows moves.

Next, we'll meet the optimizer that makes these choices, and find out what Spark does when its guesses about sizes turn out wrong.

quiz.q: A job runs a slow function of your own over 2 TB of payments and ends with `.coalesce(1).write().parquet(out)`, to get one output file. It takes hours, and Spark shows a single busy task. Why?
options: `coalesce` is narrow, so the whole last stage, slow function included, ran as one task
Writing one big file to cloud storage is slow
`coalesce(1)` shuffles all 2 TB to one executor
The driver writes the output file itself
quiz.why: `coalesce` doesn't start a new stage; it runs inside the stage before it, so that stage runs as 1 task and the slow function runs on one core. `repartition(1)` would add a shuffle instead: the stage with the function would keep its many tasks, and only the final write would run alone. `coalesce` never shuffles, and executors write the files, not the driver.

quiz.q: `groupBy(merchant_id).agg(sum(amount_cents))` reads 8 input partitions, and each partition holds payments from all 1,000 shops. How many rows do the map tasks write to shuffle files?
quiz.why: Spark adds up inside each map task first (the partial sums, lesson 3's combiner), so each of the 8 map tasks writes one row per shop it saw: 8 x 1,000 = 8,000. Without the partial sums it would be every payment. 1,000 is what the reduce side ends up with once it combines the partial sums.

quiz.q: Two tables share the key `payment_id`: one of 2 TB, one of 3 TB. You join them. Which join should Spark use?
options: Broadcast hash join, copying the 3 TB table
Broadcast hash join, with a hint on the 2 TB table
Sort-merge join, shuffling both tables by `payment_id`
Pair every row with every row, then keep the matches
quiz.why: Neither side is small enough to copy to every executor: broadcasting terabytes would overflow the driver and every executor's memory. Both sides must be partitioned by `payment_id` so that matching rows meet, which is the sort-merge join's shuffle. Pairing every row with every row (a cross join) would make billions times billions of pairs.

quiz.q: `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` is 200 and AQE is off. A `groupBy` produces 50 KB of totals. How many reduce tasks run?
options: as many as there were input partitions
quiz.why: With AQE off, Spark uses the setting as it is: 200 reduce tasks, most of them handling a few hundred bytes. With AQE on (the default), Spark would measure the 50 KB once the map tasks finish and merge the partitions into one. The number of input partitions only decides the map side.

quiz.q: From The Spark execution model: a plan has a `SortMergeJoin` with an `Exchange` under each table, and a `groupBy` after the join adds a third `Exchange`. AQE is off. How many stages does the job run?
quiz.why: Each `Exchange` cuts the plan once, and three cuts make four pieces: a stage that reads the payments, a stage that reads the shops, a stage that joins and adds up partial sums, and the final sum. `JoinDemo` showed exactly that: tasks per stage `[4, 2, 4, 4]`. The rule from The Spark execution model, stages = Exchanges + 1, holds when a plan has two inputs too.

flashcards.front: What does one map task leave on disk after a shuffle?
flashcards.back: One `.data` file with a block per reduce task, written back to back, and an `.index` file with the offsets where those blocks start and end, in the folder named by `spark.local.dir`.

flashcards.front: Which partitioner does `orderBy` use, and what extra cost does it bring?
flashcards.back: Range partitioning. Spark first runs a sampling job to choose where each range starts and ends, so an `orderBy` runs an extra job.

`repartition(n)` shuffles every row round robin into n equal partitions. `coalesce(n)` merges neighbouring partitions without a shuffle, can only lower the number, and runs the stage before it in n tasks.

flashcards.front: What is the default of `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`, and what does AQE do with it?
flashcards.back: 200. With AQE on, Spark measures the shuffle output and merges small partitions toward 64 MB each, so a high starting number is safe.

flashcards.front: When does Spark broadcast a join side on its own?
flashcards.back: When its size estimate for that side is below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, 10 MB by default. `broadcast(df)` or `/*+ BROADCAST(t) */` asks for it.

flashcards.front: What does a broadcast hash join save, and what does it cost?
flashcards.back: It saves shuffling and sorting the big table. It costs collecting the small table in the driver and keeping a copy in every executor's memory.

flashcards.front: Why does a shuffle with many reduce tasks get slow, even on small data?
flashcards.back: Each map task writes one block per reduce task, so a block's size is the map output divided by R. Many tiny blocks mean many small reads; LinkedIn measured 15% of its cluster's compute time lost waiting for them.

terms.plain: Moving every row to the task that handles its key: map tasks write rows to files on their own disk, and reduce tasks fetch them.
A file a map task writes to its local disk, holding one block of rows per reduce task, with an index file that says where each block starts.
Choosing a row's partition as hash(key) mod N, so rows with equal keys always land in the same partition.
Giving each partition one stretch of key values, chosen from a sample, so that the sorted partitions read in order give a sorted table.
Merging neighbouring partitions without a shuffle; it can only lower their number.
A join that shuffles both tables by key, sorts each partition and walks the two sorted lists together.
A join that copies the small table to every executor as a hash table and joins the big table where it lies.
The number of partitions, and so of reduce tasks, for joins and groupBy; 200 by default.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why adding `broadcast(merchants)` to one line cut the hourly report from 25 minutes to 6. Explain what Spark did before and after, in terms of shuffles.
explain_back.answer: Before, Spark planned a sort-merge join. To bring each payment together with its shop, it hash-partitioned both tables by `merchant_id`. Every map task wrote all of its payments into shuffle files on its own disk, one block per reduce task. Then every reduce task fetched its block from every map task over the network, sorted what it got and merged it with the shops. So the whole payments table was turned into bytes, written, sent and sorted on every run. Spark chose that plan because its size estimate for the filtered shops table was above the 10 MB broadcast limit: after a filter, it can't tell how many rows are left. After the hint, Spark collected the shops in the driver and sent a copy to every executor, where each task built a hash table and joined its own payments in place. The payments never moved and nothing was sorted, so the join's shuffle disappeared; the only shuffle left is the small one for the totals after it. It stays safe as long as the shops table stays small enough to copy to every executor.

deeper.body:
The shuffle in this lesson is a barrier: no reduce task starts before every map task has finished writing. That keeps recovery simple, because a failed reduce task fetches again and nothing else runs twice, and it gives batch Spark its clean stage boundaries. It also means the reduce side can't start until the slowest map task is done.

Other designs drop the barrier. BigQuery, Google's cloud service for running SQL over very large tables, moved its shuffle in 2014 to a separate tier of computers that hold the data in memory, spilling to disk only for large volumes. Because the shuffle data lives in that tier and not with the task that made it, a reduce side can read rows as soon as they are produced. BigQuery also picks the number of partitions while the query runs, since a bad choice can make a query orders of magnitude slower or make it fail.

Spark 4.3's Real-time Mode, which the Stream processing track's Spark lesson met, added pipelined shuffles for streams: both sides of the shuffle run at the same time, and rows flow between them as they're made. Batch Spark still writes every shuffle to disk between stages, which is why the first Try it found shuffle files at all.

Push-based shuffle has conditions. Spark's docs say it works only on YARN, the part of Hadoop (lesson 3's big-data system) that shares a cluster's computers among jobs, and only with the external shuffle service turned on.

Remote shuffle services are in real use. Apache Celeborn became a top-level project of the Apache Software Foundation, the non-profit that also looks after Spark, in April 2024, and its release 0.7.0 came out in August 2026. Large online companies such as Alibaba, Shopee and Bilibili run it on their clusters.

One more way to skip a shuffle: if two tables are already stored split by the same key, in pieces that match, a join can match piece with piece and never move a row. Spark calls this a storage-partitioned join, and it works with table formats such as Iceberg (lesson 11).
